title: How to Evaluate Retail Computer Vision Vendors: 10 Questions to Ask
summary: Use these questions about measurement, privacy, and scale, plus a scorecard, to evaluate computer vision platforms with confidence.
body_markdown:
A polished demo can make almost any computer[vision analytics platform](https://standard.ai/vision-analytics-by-standard-ai/) look impressive. But when you’re evaluating vendors for your retail stores, the dashboard is only part of the picture. What matters is how the data behind those insights is produced, what the platform can actually measure, and how reliably it performs in real store environments.


The right questions can help you look beyond similar-sounding features and understand what each vendor is really offering. The 10 questions below give retailers a practical framework for comparing vendors on technology, measurement capabilities, privacy practices, and support for broader rollout.


## Why Evaluating These Vendors Is Harder Than It Looks


Many computer vision analytics vendors use similar language to describe what their platforms can do: AI-powered insights, customer journeys, store intelligence, and actionable data. But similar terminology does not necessarily mean similar measurement capabilities. A website or product demo may show you the insights a platform produces without showing you much about how it generates them.


That distinction matters when you’re evaluating technology for your stores. Take dwell time. A higher density of shoppers standing near a fixture can show that people spent more time in that area, but on its own it doesn’t show that they were paying attention to the fixture. Those shoppers could be waiting in line, looking at their phones, or facing a different direction entirely. Dwell time without context is easy to mistake for engagement.


Understanding whether shoppers actually engaged takes additional context: which way they were facing, whether they interacted with products or received assistance, and where they went next. When you evaluate vendors, ask not only what a platform reports, but what evidence supports each metric.


## What to Consider When Evaluating a Vendor


Looking beyond the features presented in a demo can help your team compare vendors more effectively. Before moving beyond an initial pilot, consider how each vendor approaches:


- Measurement capabilities
- Data quality and accuracy
- Camera and infrastructure requirements
- Privacy and data practices
- Platform and use-case capabilities
- Scalability across locations
- Evidence of business value


These factors provide a starting point for comparing vendors beyond what you see in a product demo. Asking the right questions can help you dig deeper into each area and understand what a platform can actually deliver for your stores.


## 10 Questions to Ask Retail Computer Vision Analytics Vendors


Use these during vendor conversations, RFPs, or pilot reviews. For each one, look for a specific, verifiable answer rather than a general description of the platform.


### 1. Does the platform work with our existing cameras, or does it require new hardware?


**Why it matters:** Hardware requirements drive implementation cost, infrastructure planning, and how quickly you can expand to new locations. If a platform needs new sensors or cameras at every store, that cost and timeline should be clear before a rollout begins. Across 100+ locations, it can be the difference between a rollout measured in weeks and one measured in quarters.


**A strong answer:** The platform runs on your existing camera infrastructure, with little or no net-new hardware required to start.


### 2. Does it connect shopper activity across the store, or primarily count traffic and measure dwell time?


**Why it matters:** Traffic and dwell time are useful but partial. Dwell tells you a shopper paused near a display. It does not tell you whether they engaged with it, where they went next, or how that connects to a purchase. Those questions drive merchandising and staffing decisions, and[static zone heatmaps often fall short](https://standard.ai/why-traditional-heatmaps-are-failing-retailers-and-whats-next/) .


**A strong answer:** The platform connects activity across camera views to build continuous customer journeys, following a shopper through the store even when they briefly leave one camera’s view, rather than reporting isolated zone counts.


### 3. How is each metric defined and calculated?


**Why it matters:** “Engagement,” “interaction,” and “impression” can mean different things from one vendor to the next. Without clear definitions, it is hard to compare platforms, trust a number, or defend it to a CFO.


**A strong answer:** The vendor documents how each metric is calculated, what it represents, and what conditions affect it, and treats that transparency as a feature rather than a disclosure risk.


### 4. Can it distinguish customers from employees without facial recognition?


**Why it matters:** If associates are counted as shoppers, service, conversion, and staffing metrics are all affected. The method matters too. Facial recognition introduces privacy and compliance risk that many retailers will not accept, but the alternatives vary widely in accuracy.


Many platforms rely on simple rules instead: someone standing behind a register, or someone in the store longer than a set number of hours, gets classified as an employee. Those rules can filter out an associate stationed at checkout. But when that associate walks the floor to restock a shelf or help a shopper, a platform that can’t follow continuous customer journeys may count them as a shopper again, inflating traffic and engagement data.


**A strong answer:** The vendor separates customers from employees through anonymous customer segmentation, without facial recognition and without personally identifiable information. That separation holds as people move throughout the store, not just at fixed locations like the register.


**A useful follow-up:** Is the separation accurate enough to report on employee activity, such as service interactions and staffing coverage, rather than only removing employees from shopper counts?


### 5. How does measurement hold up in a real store over time?


**Why it matters:** Retail environments change constantly. Lighting shifts, fixtures move, seasonal displays appear, and stores are re-merchandised. Plenty of systems perform well in a controlled demo and degrade in a live store.


**A strong answer:** The vendor can show evidence of consistent, higher-fidelity measurement across real stores and changing conditions, with a clear explanation of how accuracy is validated.


### 6. Does the vendor collect personally identifiable information?


**Why it matters:** What a platform collects and processes affects privacy requirements, internal approvals, customer trust, and your broader approach to responsible technology. Privacy is a procurement gate at most enterprise retailers, not an afterthought.


**A strong answer:** Privacy by design. The platform produces useful behavioral insights without collecting PII and without facial recognition, so you do not have to trade responsible practice for useful data.


### 7. Can the behavioral data integrate with our existing business systems?


**Why it matters:** Understanding what happens inside a store is valuable, but connecting that behavior to sales transactions, staffing, and other business data is what makes the insights actionable. Without that integration, retailers are left with another standalone analytics tool rather than a more complete picture of store performance.


**A strong answer:** The platform provides structured behavioral data through APIs or data feeds that can be integrated with transaction, labor, merchandising, and enterprise analytics systems, allowing retailers to connect shopper behavior to business outcomes.


### 8. Can the same system support multiple retail use cases?


**Why it matters:** Retailers often want analytics across more than one function. Buying separate point solutions for traffic, merchandising, service, and retail media adds cost and creates more data to reconcile.


**A strong answer:** Store operations, merchandising, service and staffing measurement, and retail media attribution all draw on the same[retail insights](https://standard.ai/ai-retail-insights-computer-vision-store-data/) , so you can expand how you use the platform without standing up separate systems.


### 9. Can it measure in-store retail media with verified impressions rather than proxies?


**Why it matters:** Retail media measurement depends on knowing what shoppers were actually exposed to. Metrics based on aggregate traffic are a proxy. Brands funding in-store media want confirmation that a real shopper was positioned to see a placement.


**A strong answer:** The vendor can explain[how it measures in-store media exposure](https://standard.ai/vision-transforms-in-store-retail-media/) and distinguishes verified shopper impressions from estimates based on general foot traffic.


### 10. What does the path from pilot to scale look like, and how is ROI demonstrated?


**Why it matters:** A successful pilot is one data point. Before expanding, you need to know what adding locations and use cases requires, and how the vendor demonstrates business value.


**A strong answer:** The vendor offers a defined path from pilot to broader deployment, explains the resources required at each stage, and backs it with ROI evidence from comparable enterprise deployments.


## A Scorecard for Comparing Vendors


Use the questions above to build a consistent evaluation framework. A simple yes, partial, or no assessment helps your team see the differences in measurement capability, infrastructure requirements, privacy practices, and scalability.


Evaluation criterion Vendor 1 Vendor 2 Vendor 3


Works with existing cameras


Connects shopper activity across the store


Clearly defines and calculates its metrics


Distinguishes customers from employees, no facial recognition


Demonstrates performance in live retail environments


Requires no PII or facial recognition


Uses one shared measurement platform


Supports multiple retail use cases


Provides verified in-store retail media measurement


Has a defined path from pilot to scale

## Make the Decision on More Than a Vendor Demo


Evaluating retail computer vision vendors means looking past feature lists and polished dashboards. Ask how the underlying data is produced, what the platform can actually measure, how metrics are defined, how privacy is handled, and how the technology performs in real stores. Those answers give your team a clearer basis for deciding whether a platform can support the use cases, infrastructure, and scale your organization needs.


A compelling demo may get a vendor on your shortlist, but the answers to these questions should determine who earns your business.
